title: Short Stuff: Jackalope
summary: Short Stuff episode on the jackalope, the mythical creature of a jackrabbit with antlers. Josh and Chuck open with a joke about recording-day sirens, then describe what a jackalope is and its Wyoming tradition. They cover the origin story: the Herrick brothers (H. Douglas and Ralph), Wyoming taxidermists who reportedly joined a dead jackrabbit with antlers around the 1930s-40s. Roy Ball bought the original for ten dollars and displayed it in his Douglas, Wyoming hotel until it was stolen decades later and never recovered. Josh confesses to stealing a stuffed porcupine from a bar in Athens during college. The hosts discuss the Herricks selling tens of thousands of mounts, the cost to rabbits and deer, and Wall Drug's giant jackalope. They explain shope papillomavirus, which causes horn-like growths on rabbits and is unrelated to the invention, and mention Douglas's Jackalope Days, the fake hunting license, and Wyoming's failed attempts to make the jackalope the official state mythological creature. The episode closes with shout-outs and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and jackalope introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about fire sirens during past recordings and their studio history. Josh introduces the jackalope as a fake creature made by combining a rabbit or hare with antlers, common as wall art in the western US, and tied to Wyoming tradition.

segments.title: Jackalope legends and Herrick brothers origin
segments.summary: The hosts describe jackalope legends, including singing voices and a supposed link to Bigfoot. They note the origin story is credited to the Herrick brothers of Wyoming, and that Wyoming has repeatedly tried and failed to make the jackalope its official state mythological creature.

segments.title: Herrick brothers biographies and the first jackalope
segments.summary: Chuck gives background on H. Douglas Herrick and his brother Ralph, Wyoming taxidermists. Legend says one brother returned from a hunt with a dead jackrabbit, which was placed against a pair of antlers, sparking the idea to make the first jackalope, around the 1930s to 1940s.

segments.title: Roy Ball's hotel and the stolen original
segments.summary: Roy Ball, who ran a hotel in Douglas, Wyoming, bought the original jackalope for ten dollars and displayed it for three or four decades. It was later stolen and never recovered.

segments.title: Josh's college porcupine theft
segments.summary: Josh confesses that in college in Athens, he and friends took a stuffed porcupine from a bar, kept it for about six months, then returned it anonymously. The hosts reminisce about the bar scene in Athens.

segments.title: Commercial production, rabbit deaths, and Wall Drug
segments.summary: The Herrick family began making and selling jackalopes, reportedly tens of thousands, at a cost to many rabbits and deer. Wall Drug in South Dakota became a distributor with a giant jackalope, and the Herricks' son told the New York Times in 2003 that about 1,500 to 2,000 were sold a year there.

segments.title: Shope papillomavirus and rabbit horns
segments.summary: The hosts explain that shope papillomavirus, related to HPV, causes tumors that look like horns on rabbits. They note that the first sightings of horned rabbits date to the 16th or 17th centuries, and that this condition is unrelated to the jackalope's invention.

segments.title: Douglas Jackalope Days, licenses, and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts mention Douglas, Wyoming as the jackalope's home, Wyoming's fake jackalope hunting license, and Jackalope Days festival. They give shout-outs and close the episode.
